title: Esta vs Está: This or Is in Spanish?
seo_title: Esta vs Está: This or Is in Spanish?
meta_description: Esta vs está: esta means this (a demonstrative) and está means is (from estar). Stress, rules, the esta/ésta question, common mistakes and a quick quiz.
excerpt: “This” or “is”? The stress, and the accent, make the difference.

body_html:
Esta vs está is a pair where the accent changes both the meaning and the pronunciation. Esta (stress on the first syllable, ES-ta) means “this” and goes with feminine nouns: esta casa. Está (stress on the last syllable, es-TÁ) means “is” and comes from the verb estar: La casa está cerca. Unlike tu/tú, these two actually sound different, so listening carefully helps you spell them right.

Quick answer
  • Esta = this (feminine): esta mañana, esta chica.
  • Está = is (he/she/it/you formal), from estar: Está cansada.
  • Stress: ESta vs esTÁ.
  • Plural: estas (these) vs están (they are).
{{toc}}

Esta vs está: the core rule

EstaEstá
Meaningthis (feminine)is (he, she, it, you formal)
Word typeDemonstrativeVerb (estar)
StressES-taes-TÁ
Pluralestasestán
ExampleEsta sopa es casera.La sopa está caliente.

The accent on está follows the regular stress rules: it ends in a vowel and is stressed on the last syllable, so it needs a written accent. The RAE dictionary lists está as the third-person present of estar.

Esta: this

  • Esta noche salimos. We’re going out tonight.
  • ¿Cuánto cuesta esta camiseta? How much is this T-shirt?
  • Esta es mi amiga Laura. This is my friend Laura.
  • Estas flores son para ti. These flowers are for you.

With masculine nouns, the form is este: este libro. See {{link:este-ese-aquel|este, ese, aquel}}.

Está: is

  • ¿Dónde está el baño? Where is the bathroom?
  • Mi madre está enferma. My mother is ill.
  • La comida está lista. The food is ready.
  • Está lloviendo. It’s raining.

Estar is used for location, states and the progressive tense. If you’re unsure when to use it rather than ser, see {{link:ser-vs-estar|ser vs estar}}.

{{image:2}}

What about ésta?

You may see ésta with an accent on the first syllable in older books, used when the word replaces a noun: Prefiero ésta. Since 2010, the RAE recommends writing it without an accent: Prefiero esta. So in modern Spanish there are only two forms to know: esta and está.

Both in one sentence

The two words often appear together, which makes great practice:

  • Esta habitación está muy limpia. This room is very clean.
  • Esta mañana mi jefe está de buen humor. This morning my boss is in a good mood.
  • ¿Esta silla está libre? Is this chair free?
{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Why this is tricky for learners

Learners often don’t notice word stress when reading Spanish, so esta and está look like the same word with a random mark. In reality, the accent tells you where to put the stress, and the meanings are completely different. Reading aloud helps: say ESta and esTÁ clearly and the spelling follows. When typing quickly, it is easy to skip the accent on está, and spell-checkers won’t always catch it because esta is also a real word.

A quick mental shortcut

Replace the word with “this” or “is”. If “this” fits and a feminine noun follows (or is understood), write esta. If “is” fits, write está. Another test: change to the plural. If it becomes estas, it was esta; if it becomes están, it was está.

Real conversation

  • A: ¿Esta es tu chamarra? (Is this your jacket?)
  • B: Sí, gracias. ¿Dónde estaba? (Yes, thanks. Where was it?)
  • A: Estaba en la silla. ¡Y está mojada! (It was on the chair. And it’s wet!)

Texting and typing tips

On a phone, hold down the a key to get á. On a Mac, type Option + E and then a. Many Spanish keyboards also suggest está automatically, but because esta is a real word, autocorrect will not always fix your mistake. In casual chats, native speakers often skip the accent and nobody minds. In emails, CVs and anything you publish, take a second to check every esta: is it “this” or “is”? It is one of the quickest ways to make your written Spanish look careful and professional.

A final reminder: the masculine pair works the same way, este (this) versus esté (subjunctive of estar): Espero que esté bien (I hope he’s well).

Está noche voy al cine.Esta noche voy al cine.“This night”: esta
Esta muy bien.Está muy bien.Verb: está

Try it yourself

  1. This city is beautiful. (Esta ciudad es preciosa.)
  2. Where is your sister? (¿Dónde está tu hermana?)
  3. This coffee is cold. (Este café está frío.) Careful: café is masculine!
  4. This week I’m very busy. (Esta semana estoy muy ocupado.)
  5. Is this table free? (¿Esta mesa está libre?)

All accent pairs in {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

“This”: esta, stressed at the start. “Is”: está, stressed at the end. Say them aloud, and your spelling will follow your ear.

faq.q: What is the difference between esta and está?
faq.a: Esta means this and goes with feminine nouns. Está means is and comes from the verb estar. They are also pronounced with different stress.

faq.q: Does ésta still have an accent?
faq.a: No. Since 2010 the RAE recommends writing demonstratives without an accent: Prefiero esta.

faq.q: How do I know when to write está?
faq.a: If you can translate it as “is”, it is the verb estar and needs the accent: ¿Dónde está?
